question_text:
A 74-year-old man is brought to an emergency department in Ballina, NSW, after feeling faint all morning. He is pale and sweaty. Pulse 36/min and regular, BP 82/50 mmHg. His ECG shows sinus bradycardia at 36/min with a normal QRS. He takes no rate-slowing medicines and has not had a cardiac transplant.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate initial drug treatment?
options: Intravenous adrenaline infusion as the first drug
Intravenous adenosine 6 mg
Intravenous amiodarone 300 mg
Observation only because sinus rhythm is present
Intravenous atropine 500–600 micrograms, repeated every 3–5 minutes as needed
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

E. Intravenous atropine 500–600 micrograms, repeated every 3–5 minutes as needed

---

He has a bradyarrhythmia with adverse signs (systolic BP <90 mmHg, heart rate <40/min). ANZCOR Guideline 11.9 says atropine is the first treatment: 500–600 micrograms IV, repeated every 3–5 minutes up to 3 mg. If this fails, low-dose adrenaline is the second-line drug, with pacing for patients who do not respond or who are at high risk of asystole.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Bradycardia with adverse signs: give IV atropine 500–600 mcg (up to 3 mg), then adrenaline or pacing if that fails.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "ANZCOR Guideline 11.9 – Managing Acute Dysrhythmias", "url": "https://www.anzcor.org/home/adult-advanced-life-support/guideline-11-9-managing-acute-dysrhythmias"}
subtopic: Symptomatic bradycardia: IV atropine first

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: ANZCOR lists adrenaline as second-line, after atropine fails.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Adenosine is for regular narrow-complex tachycardia, not bradycardia.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Amiodarone is an antiarrhythmic for tachyarrhythmias and would worsen bradycardia.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Bradycardia with hypotension and heart rate <40/min needs immediate treatment.

key_takeaways: Bradycardia with adverse signs: give IV atropine 500–600 mcg (up to 3 mg), then adrenaline or pacing if that fails.
guideline_reference: {"name": "ANZCOR Guideline 11.9 – Managing Acute Dysrhythmias", "url": "https://www.anzcor.org/home/adult-advanced-life-support/guideline-11-9-managing-acute-dysrhythmias"}

question_text:
A 66-year-old woman presents to an emergency department in Warrnambool, Vic, with palpitations for three hours. She is alert, BP 128/78 mmHg. ECG shows a regular narrow-complex tachycardia at 150/min. A modified Valsalva manoeuvre has no effect. During IV adenosine 6 mg, the rhythm strip shows the ventricular rate slow briefly, revealing regular saw-tooth atrial activity at about 300/min, before the tachycardia at 150/min returns.

Which one of the following is the most likely rhythm?
options: Atrial flutter with 2:1 atrioventricular conduction
AV nodal re-entry tachycardia
AV re-entry tachycardia via an accessory pathway
Sinus tachycardia
Ventricular tachycardia
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

A. Atrial flutter with 2:1 atrioventricular conduction

---

ANZCOR Guideline 11.9 notes that if the ventricular rate slows briefly with adenosine but the arrhythmia continues, you should look for atrial flutter or another atrial tachycardia. Saw-tooth flutter waves at about 300/min with a ventricular rate of 150/min indicate atrial flutter with 2:1 conduction. Adenosine blocks the AV node but does not end a rhythm generated within the atria.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
If adenosine only briefly slows a regular narrow-complex tachycardia and reveals saw-tooth waves, it is atrial flutter.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "ANZCOR Guideline 11.9 – Managing Acute Dysrhythmias", "url": "https://www.anzcor.org/home/adult-advanced-life-support/guideline-11-9-managing-acute-dysrhythmias"}
subtopic: Regular narrow-complex tachycardia: adenosine unmasks atrial flutter

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: AVNRT depends on the AV node and usually terminates with adenosine rather than revealing flutter waves.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: AVRT also uses the AV node and usually terminates with adenosine.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: There are saw-tooth flutter waves rather than P waves, and the rate is fixed at 150/min.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: VT is a broad-complex tachycardia; this QRS is narrow and adenosine revealed flutter waves.

key_takeaways: If adenosine only briefly slows a regular narrow-complex tachycardia and reveals saw-tooth waves, it is atrial flutter.
guideline_reference: {"name": "ANZCOR Guideline 11.9 – Managing Acute Dysrhythmias", "url": "https://www.anzcor.org/home/adult-advanced-life-support/guideline-11-9-managing-acute-dysrhythmias"}

question_text:
A 24-year-old man with known Wolff–Parkinson–White pattern presents to an emergency department in Newcastle, NSW, with palpitations for one hour. He is alert, BP 112/70 mmHg. ECG shows an irregularly irregular broad-complex tachycardia at 210–250/min, with QRS complexes that vary in width from beat to beat.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate interpretation and plan?
options: AF with bundle branch block; give IV verapamil for rate control
Monomorphic VT; give IV adenosine 6 mg to clarify the rhythm
Pre-excited AF; avoid AV nodal blockers and plan cardioversion
AF with rapid ventricular response; give IV digoxin loading
Sinus tachycardia with aberrancy; give a fluid bolus
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

C. Pre-excited AF; avoid AV nodal blockers and plan cardioversion

---

An irregular broad-complex tachycardia with varying QRS width in a patient with WPW suggests atrial fibrillation conducting down the accessory pathway. ANZCOR Guideline 11.9 states that if pre-excited AF is suspected, adenosine, digoxin, verapamil and diltiazem should be avoided. These drugs block the AV node and cause a relative increase in pre-excitation, which can degenerate to VF. Electrical cardioversion is usually the safest treatment.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Pre-excited AF (WPW with irregular broad complexes): avoid AV nodal blockers. Electrical cardioversion is usually safest.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "ANZCOR Guideline 11.9 – Managing Acute Dysrhythmias", "url": "https://www.anzcor.org/home/adult-advanced-life-support/guideline-11-9-managing-acute-dysrhythmias"}
subtopic: Irregular broad-complex tachycardia in WPW: avoid AV nodal blockers

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: In WPW, AV nodal blockers can accelerate conduction down the accessory pathway.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: The rhythm is irregular, and adenosine is contraindicated in pre-excited AF.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Digoxin is specifically listed to avoid in pre-excited AF.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: The rhythm is irregularly irregular and at 250/min, so it is not sinus.

key_takeaways: Pre-excited AF (WPW with irregular broad complexes): avoid AV nodal blockers. Electrical cardioversion is usually safest.
guideline_reference: {"name": "ANZCOR Guideline 11.9 – Managing Acute Dysrhythmias", "url": "https://www.anzcor.org/home/adult-advanced-life-support/guideline-11-9-managing-acute-dysrhythmias"}

question_text:
A 59-year-old man in Bendigo, Vic, has had palpitations for about five days. ECG shows atrial fibrillation at 105/min. He is stable, with BP 134/82 mmHg. He is not taking an anticoagulant. The cardiology team would like to restore sinus rhythm during this admission rather than wait weeks.

Which one of the following investigations is required before early cardioversion?
options: Transthoracic echocardiography
Serial high-sensitivity troponin
Transoesophageal echocardiography
Thyroid function tests
24-hour Holter monitoring
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

C. Transoesophageal echocardiography

---

ANZCOR Guideline 11.9 states that patients who have been in AF for more than 48 hours should not have electrical or chemical cardioversion until they are fully anticoagulated, unless transoesophageal echocardiography has shown there is no atrial clot. Transthoracic echo cannot reliably exclude left atrial appendage thrombus.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
AF for more than 48 hours: cardiovert only after full anticoagulation or after TOE excludes atrial clot.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "ANZCOR Guideline 11.9 – Managing Acute Dysrhythmias", "url": "https://www.anzcor.org/home/adult-advanced-life-support/guideline-11-9-managing-acute-dysrhythmias"}
subtopic: AF for more than 48 hours: TOE before early cardioversion

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: TTE cannot reliably exclude left atrial appendage thrombus.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Troponin does not assess the risk of thromboembolism from cardioversion.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: TFTs are useful for finding a cause, but they do not make cardioversion safe.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: Holter monitoring is not needed. AF is already documented.

key_takeaways: AF for more than 48 hours: cardiovert only after full anticoagulation or after TOE excludes atrial clot.
guideline_reference: {"name": "ANZCOR Guideline 11.9 – Managing Acute Dysrhythmias", "url": "https://www.anzcor.org/home/adult-advanced-life-support/guideline-11-9-managing-acute-dysrhythmias"}

question_text:
A 45-year-old woman in Launceston, Tas, has just finished 12 weeks of sofosbuvir/velpatasvir for chronic hepatitis C. She has no cirrhosis. She took every dose, and her ALT is now normal. She asks how she will know she is cured.

Which one of the following tests best confirms cure?
options: HCV RNA by PCR at least 12 weeks after treatment
HCV antibody at least 12 weeks after treatment
HCV RNA by PCR on the last day of treatment
ALT at least 12 weeks after treatment
HCV genotype at the end of treatment
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

A. HCV RNA by PCR at least 12 weeks after treatment

---

The Australian HCV guidelines define cure (sustained virological response, SVR12) as undetectable HCV RNA on a highly sensitive PCR assay at least 12 weeks after DAA therapy finishes. Late relapse after SVR is very uncommon. Anti-HCV antibodies are expected to stay positive and do not indicate active infection.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Hepatitis C cure is SVR12: undetectable HCV RNA at least 12 weeks after DAA treatment ends.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "Australian recommendations for the management of hepatitis C virus infection: Post-treatment follow-up (Confirm SVR)", "url": "https://hepcguidelines.org.au/post-treatment-follow-up/"}
subtopic: Hepatitis C cure: HCV RNA at least 12 weeks after treatment (SVR12)

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Antibodies stay positive after cure, so they cannot confirm it.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: An end-of-treatment result does not rule out relapse. Cure is defined by the result at 12 weeks.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: ALT is useful for follow-up but does not confirm viral cure.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: Genotype does not assess response to treatment.

key_takeaways: Hepatitis C cure is SVR12: undetectable HCV RNA at least 12 weeks after DAA treatment ends.
guideline_reference: {"name": "Australian recommendations for the management of hepatitis C virus infection: Post-treatment follow-up (Confirm SVR)", "url": "https://hepcguidelines.org.au/post-treatment-follow-up/"}

question_text:
A 52-year-old man in Wollongong, NSW, was treated for hepatitis C three years ago. HCV RNA was undetectable 12 weeks after treatment, and he has no cirrhosis. A recent insurance medical showed a positive HCV antibody. He has not injected drugs since treatment. Today his HCV RNA is undetectable and his ALT is 24 U/L.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate interpretation?
options: Relapse of hepatitis C requiring retreatment
Reinfection requiring retreatment
Protective immunity against future HCV infection
Persistent antibody after cure; he does not have active infection and is not immune to reinfection
A false-positive antibody result that should be investigated with a liver biopsy
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

D. Persistent antibody after cure; he does not have active infection and is not immune to reinfection

---

The Australian HCV guidelines state that anti-HCV antibodies are expected to persist after SVR. They do not mean active infection, and they do not give immunity to reinfection. People without cirrhosis whose LFTs are normal after SVR do not need further specialist liver follow-up. Future testing for reinfection must use HCV RNA, not antibody.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
After HCV cure, antibodies stay positive. Use HCV RNA to test for reinfection.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "Australian recommendations for the management of hepatitis C virus infection: Post-treatment follow-up (Confirm SVR)", "url": "https://hepcguidelines.org.au/post-treatment-follow-up/"}
subtopic: Positive HCV antibody after documented cure

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Relapse means return of detectable HCV RNA after SVR; his RNA is undetectable, and relapse after SVR12 is very rare.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Reinfection is diagnosed by detectable HCV RNA (antibody stays positive regardless); his RNA is undetectable.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Antibodies do not protect against reinfection.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: The antibody is expected after past infection, and a biopsy is not indicated.

key_takeaways: After HCV cure, antibodies stay positive. Use HCV RNA to test for reinfection.
guideline_reference: {"name": "Australian recommendations for the management of hepatitis C virus infection: Post-treatment follow-up (Confirm SVR)", "url": "https://hepcguidelines.org.au/post-treatment-follow-up/"}

question_text:
A 21-year-old woman in Townsville, Qld, was treated with doxycycline for 7 days for genital chlamydia found on screening. She is not pregnant, and her symptoms have gone. Her partner has also been treated. She asks whether she needs another test.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate follow-up testing?
options: Test of cure NAAT one week after treatment
Repeat chlamydia NAAT at 3 months to detect reinfection
No further testing at any time
Chlamydia serology
Pelvic ultrasound
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

B. Repeat chlamydia NAAT at 3 months to detect reinfection

---

The Australian STI Management Guidelines say a test of cure is not routinely recommended for chlamydia, except in pregnancy and for anorectal infection treated with azithromycin. Reinfection is common, so retesting at 3 months is recommended.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
After treating uncomplicated chlamydia, retest at 3 months for reinfection. A routine test of cure is not needed.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "Australian STI Management Guidelines. Chlamydia", "url": "https://sti.guidelines.org.au/sexually-transmissible-infections/chlamydia/"}
subtopic: Treated chlamydia: retest for reinfection at 3 months

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Testing too early can give a false-positive result from persistent DNA, and a test of cure is not routinely needed.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Retesting at 3 months is recommended because reinfection is common.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Serology is not used for diagnosis or follow-up.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: Ultrasound is not indicated for uncomplicated infection.

key_takeaways: After treating uncomplicated chlamydia, retest at 3 months for reinfection. A routine test of cure is not needed.
guideline_reference: {"name": "Australian STI Management Guidelines. Chlamydia", "url": "https://sti.guidelines.org.au/sexually-transmissible-infections/chlamydia/"}

question_text:
A 58-year-old woman in Orange, NSW, has fatigue and tingling in her feet. She eats a mixed diet and takes no medicines. She has hypothyroidism and vitiligo.

Investigations:
- Haemoglobin 104 g/L, MCV 108 fL
- Serum B12 90 pmol/L (>150)
- Folate and iron studies normal

Which one of the following investigations is most appropriate to establish the cause?
options: Schilling test
Bone marrow biopsy
Coeliac serology as the only test
Serum homocysteine alone
Anti-intrinsic factor antibodies
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

E. Anti-intrinsic factor antibodies

---

With no dietary or drug cause and with other autoimmune disease, autoimmune gastritis (pernicious anaemia) is likely. Australian Prescriber recommends testing for anti-intrinsic factor antibodies when autoimmune gastritis is suspected. If these are negative, anti-parietal cell antibodies, gastrin and gastroscopy should be considered. The cause matters because B12 absorption is irreversibly impaired in pernicious anaemia, so oral B12 is unreliable and IM treatment is needed.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
If B12 deficiency suggests autoimmune gastritis, test anti-intrinsic factor antibodies. Pernicious anaemia needs IM B12.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "Australian Prescriber. Vitamin B12 deficiency: testing and treatment", "url": "https://australianprescriber.tg.org.au/articles/vitamin-B12-deficiency-testing-and-treatment.html"}
subtopic: Vitamin B12 deficiency: anti-intrinsic factor antibodies for suspected autoimmune gastritis

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: The Schilling test is no longer available in Australia; antibody testing has replaced it.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Marrow examination is only needed if there are other cytopenias or features suggesting a primary marrow disorder; B12 deficiency is diagnosed on blood tests.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: This could be considered, but the autoimmune history points to autoimmune gastritis first.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Homocysteine supports the diagnosis of deficiency but does not identify the cause.

key_takeaways: If B12 deficiency suggests autoimmune gastritis, test anti-intrinsic factor antibodies. Pernicious anaemia needs IM B12.
guideline_reference: {"name": "Australian Prescriber. Vitamin B12 deficiency: testing and treatment", "url": "https://australianprescriber.tg.org.au/articles/vitamin-B12-deficiency-testing-and-treatment.html"}

question_text:
A 70-year-old man is admitted to a hospital in Gosford, NSW, with pneumonia and sepsis. His baseline creatinine from two months ago is 90 µmol/L. On day 2 his creatinine is 200 µmol/L. Urine output has averaged 0.4 mL/kg/h over the last 8 hours. He is not on dialysis.

Which one of the following is the correct KDIGO stage of his acute kidney injury?
options: Stage 1
Stage 3
Stage 2
Not AKI because urine output is above 0.3 mL/kg/h
AKI cannot be staged without a 24-hour urine collection
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

C. Stage 2

---

KDIGO stages AKI by the worse of the creatinine and urine output criteria. Stage 1 is creatinine 1.5–1.9 times baseline (or a rise of ≥26.5 µmol/L), or urine output <0.5 mL/kg/h for 6–12 hours. Stage 2 is creatinine 2.0–2.9 times baseline, or <0.5 mL/kg/h for ≥12 hours. Stage 3 is creatinine ≥3.0 times baseline (or ≥353.6 µmol/L), urine output <0.3 mL/kg/h for ≥24 hours or anuria for ≥12 hours, or starting kidney replacement therapy. A creatinine of 200/90 is 2.2 times baseline, which is stage 2. The urine output of 0.4 mL/kg/h for 8 hours would only meet stage 1.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
KDIGO AKI stage is set by the worse of creatinine (1.5–1.9×, 2.0–2.9×, ≥3×) and urine output.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "KDIGO Clinical Practice Guideline for Acute Kidney Injury (2012)", "url": "https://kdigo.org/wp-content/uploads/2016/10/KDIGO-2012-AKI-Guideline-English.pdf"}
subtopic: Staging acute kidney injury by KDIGO criteria

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: The urine output criterion alone would be stage 1, but the creatinine rise of 2.2 times baseline makes it stage 2.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Creatinine is not ≥3 times baseline, he does not meet the stage 3 urine output criteria, and he is not on kidney replacement therapy.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Creatinine criteria alone define and stage AKI; a urine output above 0.3 mL/kg/h does not exclude it (and below 0.5 mL/kg/h for 6 hours already meets stage 1).
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: Staging uses creatinine and hourly urine output.

key_takeaways: KDIGO AKI stage is set by the worse of creatinine (1.5–1.9×, 2.0–2.9×, ≥3×) and urine output.
guideline_reference: {"name": "KDIGO Clinical Practice Guideline for Acute Kidney Injury (2012)", "url": "https://kdigo.org/wp-content/uploads/2016/10/KDIGO-2012-AKI-Guideline-English.pdf"}

question_text:
A 34-year-old nurse in Brisbane, Qld, had a needlestick injury two hours ago from a patient known to be HBsAg-positive. She is documented as a persistent non-responder to hepatitis B vaccine: anti-HBs stayed <10 mIU/mL after a full course and three further doses, and she has tested negative for hepatitis B infection.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate hepatitis B prophylaxis?
options: No prophylaxis because she has been vaccinated
A single booster dose of hepatitis B vaccine alone
Start tenofovir post-exposure prophylaxis
Hepatitis B immunoglobulin as soon as possible, within 72 hours
Wait for her anti-HBs result before deciding
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

D. Hepatitis B immunoglobulin as soon as possible, within 72 hours

---

The Australian Immunisation Handbook says persistent non-responders are probably not protected and should be told they need hepatitis B immunoglobulin within 72 hours of any parenteral or mucosal exposure to hepatitis B virus. Its post-exposure prophylaxis table covers exposure to an HBsAg-positive source. HBV and HIV/HCV baseline testing and follow-up also apply.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Persistent HBV vaccine non-responders exposed to HBsAg need HBIG within 72 hours.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "Australian Immunisation Handbook. Non-responders to hepatitis B vaccine are recommended to receive further doses and serological testing", "url": "https://immunisationhandbook.health.gov.au/recommendations/non-responders-to-hepatitis-b-vaccine-are-recommended-to-receive-further-doses-and-serological-testing"}
subtopic: Persistent hepatitis B vaccine non-responder after a needlestick: HBIG within 72 hours

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Vaccination only protects people who respond; a documented persistent non-responder (anti-HBs <10 mIU/mL after 6 doses) has no reliable protection.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: A booster will not give immediate protection to a known non-responder.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Antivirals are not the recommended hepatitis B post-exposure prophylaxis.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: Her non-response is already documented, and the 72-hour window must not be missed.

key_takeaways: Persistent HBV vaccine non-responders exposed to HBsAg need HBIG within 72 hours.

question_text:
An 86-year-old woman in Bundaberg, Qld, is brought in with three days of nausea, confusion and yellow-tinged vision. She takes digoxin 125 micrograms daily for atrial fibrillation. Her furosemide dose was recently increased, and she has had diarrhoea. Pulse 38/min with intermittent junctional rhythm, BP 86/50 mmHg.

Investigations:
- Serum digoxin 3.4 nmol/L
- Potassium 5.9 mmol/L
- Creatinine 190 µmol/L (baseline 95)

Which one of the following is the most appropriate specific treatment?
options: IV calcium gluconate for the hyperkalaemia
Haemodialysis to remove digoxin
Activated charcoal 50 g
Digoxin immune Fab, 1 vial (40 mg) IV over 30 minutes
Stop digoxin and observe without other treatment
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

D. Digoxin immune Fab, 1 vial (40 mg) IV over 30 minutes

---

This is chronic digoxin accumulation (worse kidney function, diuretics) with cardiovascular compromise (bradycardia and hypotension). Queensland Poisons Information Centre antidote guidance for chronic digoxin accumulation with compromise is digoxin immune Fab, 1 vial (40 mg) diluted in 100 mL saline over 30 minutes. Chronic accumulation is more common than acute overdose.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Chronic digoxin toxicity with compromise: digoxin Fab, 1 vial (40 mg) IV over 30 minutes (Qld PIC).

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "Queensland Poisons Information Centre. Antidote stocking recommendations: Digoxin Immune Fab", "url": "https://www.poisonsinfo.health.qld.gov.au/for-health-professionals/antidote-stocking-recommendations/digoxin-immune-fab"}
subtopic: Chronic digoxin toxicity with compromise: digoxin immune Fab

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Calcium is not the specific treatment, and digoxin Fab treats the hyperkalaemia caused by digoxin.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Digoxin has a large volume of distribution and is not removed effectively by dialysis.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Charcoal is for recent acute ingestion, not chronic accumulation.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: She has bradycardia with hypotension, which needs antidote treatment.

key_takeaways: Chronic digoxin toxicity with compromise: digoxin Fab, 1 vial (40 mg) IV over 30 minutes (Qld PIC).
guideline_reference: {"name": "Queensland Poisons Information Centre. Antidote stocking recommendations: Digoxin Immune Fab", "url": "https://www.poisonsinfo.health.qld.gov.au/for-health-professionals/antidote-stocking-recommendations/digoxin-immune-fab"}

question_text:
A 72-year-old woman with COPD sees her GP in Port Macquarie, NSW, with four days of increased breathlessness and more sputum, which has changed from white to green. She is not febrile. SpO2 93% on room air, respiratory rate 20/min. She is not drowsy. Her GP plans to increase her bronchodilators and start oral prednisolone.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate antibiotic plan?
options: No antibiotics because she is afebrile
Oral amoxicillin/clavulanate for 14 days
IV ceftriaxone
Oral azithromycin for 3 days
Oral amoxycillin or doxycycline for 5 days
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

E. Oral amoxycillin or doxycycline for 5 days

---

COPD-X recommends antibiotics (amoxycillin or doxycycline for 5 days) for exacerbations with clinical features of infection, such as increased sputum volume with a change in colour, and/or fever. Treatment also includes bronchodilators and a short course of oral corticosteroids.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
COPD exacerbation with purulent sputum: amoxycillin or doxycycline for 5 days.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "Lung Foundation Australia. COPD-X Plan: X – Manage exacerbations", "url": "https://copdx.org.au/copd-x-plan/x-manage-exacerbations/"}
subtopic: Infective COPD exacerbation: 5 days of amoxycillin or doxycycline

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: A change in sputum colour with increased volume is enough to indicate infection.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: COPD-X recommends amoxycillin or doxycycline for 5 days; amoxicillin-clavulanate for 14 days is broader and longer than needed, with more adverse effects.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: She is managing at home with SpO2 93% and no drowsiness; IV antibiotics are for hospitalised patients unable to take oral therapy or with severe disease.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Azithromycin is not the recommended first-line choice for an exacerbation.

key_takeaways: COPD exacerbation with purulent sputum: amoxycillin or doxycycline for 5 days.

question_text:
A 68-year-old man with COPD is admitted to a hospital in Mildura, Vic, with five days of worsening breathlessness and new right-sided pleuritic chest pain. Sputum is unchanged and white, and he is afebrile. He had a total knee replacement four weeks ago. Pulse 112/min, SpO2 87% on room air. Chest X-ray shows hyperinflation only.

Which one of the following investigations is most important next?
options: Sputum culture
Spirometry
CT pulmonary angiography
D-dimer alone to decide whether to image
Repeat chest X-ray in 24 hours
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

C. CT pulmonary angiography

---

COPD-X cites a systematic review in which 16% of patients hospitalised with a COPD exacerbation who had CT pulmonary angiography were found to have a pulmonary embolism. With no infective features, pleuritic pain, tachycardia, hypoxaemia and recent major orthopaedic surgery, PE must be actively excluded. Here the best test is CTPA.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
In a COPD exacerbation without infective features, especially with pleuritic pain or VTE risk, look for PE (CTPA).

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "Lung Foundation Australia. COPD-X Plan: X – Manage exacerbations", "url": "https://copdx.org.au/copd-x-plan/x-manage-exacerbations/"}
subtopic: COPD exacerbation without infective features: consider pulmonary embolism

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: There are no infective features, and the result will not exclude PE.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Spirometry is not done during an acute exacerbation.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: With a high pre-test probability, go straight to imaging.

question_text:
A 29-year-old medical student in Adelaide, SA, completed a 3-dose hepatitis B vaccine course as a child. Pre-placement anti-HBs was <10 mIU/mL, so she had a single booster dose. Four weeks after the booster, anti-HBs is still <10 mIU/mL.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate next step?
options: Declare her immune because she completed a childhood course
Give a full repeat 3-dose course without further testing
Give hepatitis B immunoglobulin now as a precaution
Test HBsAg and anti-HBc; if negative, give 2 more doses and recheck anti-HBs
Recheck anti-HBs in 12 months before any further doses
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

D. Test HBsAg and anti-HBc; if negative, give 2 more doses and recheck anti-HBs

---

The Australian Immunisation Handbook advises that people who still have anti-HBs <10 mIU/mL after a booster should be tested for hepatitis B infection. If that is negative, they are recommended to have 2 more doses 1 month apart, with the booster counted as the first of the 3 repeat doses. Anti-HBs is rechecked at least 4 weeks after the last dose. Persistent non-responders need HBIG after any exposure.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
No response after a hepatitis B booster: exclude infection, then give 2 more doses and recheck anti-HBs at 4 weeks or more.

---

question_text:
A 77-year-old woman in Lismore, NSW, has had prochlorperazine 5 mg three times daily for dizziness for the past 10 weeks. Her daughter has noticed repetitive lip-smacking, chewing movements and tongue protrusion over the last two weeks. Her gait and arm movements are otherwise normal.

Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Acute dystonic reaction
Tardive dyskinesia
Drug-induced parkinsonism
Akathisia
Huntington disease
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

B. Tardive dyskinesia

---

Australian Prescriber notes that tardive movement disorders need a minimum drug exposure of three months, or one month in adults over 60. Antiemetics such as metoclopramide and prochlorperazine are among the drugs most often responsible. Tardive dyskinesias are typically orobuccolingual, as in this patient.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Orobuccolingual dyskinesia after ≥1 month of a dopamine blocker in a person over 60 suggests tardive dyskinesia.

---

incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Akathisia is a subjective restlessness with an urge to move.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: Onset at 77 shortly after a dopamine blocker points to the drug.

question_text:
A 41-year-old woman in Hobart, Tas, with immune thrombocytopenia that has not responded to treatment is booked for elective laparoscopic splenectomy in five weeks. She is up to date with her routine adult vaccines but has never had additional pneumococcal, meningococcal or Hib vaccines.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate vaccination plan?
options: Give the asplenia vaccines on the day after surgery
Give the asplenia vaccines 6 months after surgery
No vaccines are needed if she takes lifelong antibiotic prophylaxis
Give the asplenia vaccines now, completing them 2 weeks before surgery
Give influenza vaccine only, as the others are already up to date
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

D. Give the asplenia vaccines now, completing them 2 weeks before surgery

---

The Australian Immunisation Handbook recommends that people having a planned splenectomy receive all scheduled vaccines at least 2 weeks before surgery, when possible. This includes extra doses of pneumococcal, meningococcal (MenACWY and MenB) and Hib vaccines and annual influenza vaccine, to optimise the immune response. After an emergency splenectomy, vaccination is ideally delayed until 2 weeks after surgery.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Planned splenectomy: complete asplenia vaccines at least 2 weeks before surgery.

---

question_text:
A 30-year-old man from a remote station in western Queensland had an emergency splenectomy in Townsville five days ago after a motorbike crash. He is recovering well and wants to go home tomorrow. He lives 900 km away, and the team thinks he is unlikely to return for review.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate timing of his asplenia vaccines?
options: Give the vaccines before discharge because follow-up is unlikely
Delay vaccination until a 2-week review regardless of circumstances
No vaccination because the spleen was removed after trauma, not disease
Give only antibiotic prophylaxis and no vaccines
Vaccinate after 6 months
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

A. Give the vaccines before discharge because follow-up is unlikely

---

The Handbook advises that after emergency splenectomy, vaccines are ideally given 2 weeks after surgery because antibody responses, especially to pneumococcal vaccines, are better then. If there is concern that the patient may not return or may be lost to follow-up, vaccines may be given once the person is stable and before discharge. The risk of infection is highest in the first 1–2 years.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
After emergency splenectomy, vaccinate at 2 weeks, or before discharge if he may be lost to follow-up.

---

question_text:
A 36-year-old woman was a restrained driver in a crash near Toowoomba, Qld. CT on arrival showed an AAST grade IV splenic laceration without active extravasation. She has stayed haemodynamically stable and is being managed non-operatively in the high dependency unit. Today is day 3, and her haemoglobin is stable.

Which one of the following investigations is recommended now?
options: Repeat CT angiography of the abdomen
No imaging if she remains stable
Abdominal ultrasound only
Diagnostic laparoscopy
Repeat CT only at 6 weeks before she returns to sport
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

A. Repeat CT angiography of the abdomen

---

The Queensland adult blunt splenic injury guideline recommends that high-grade injuries (AAST grade IV–V) be managed in HDU or ICU with repeat CT angiography 3 to 5 days after injury. This looks for delayed vascular injury such as pseudoaneurysm, which may need embolisation. Grade III injuries are managed on a specialised ward, with repeat CTA considered according to clinical need.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Grade IV–V blunt splenic injury managed non-operatively: HDU or ICU care and repeat CTA at days 3–5.

---

question_text:
A 63-year-old man in Toowong, Qld, had a PSA of 4.6 µg/L, confirmed on repeat testing. Multiparametric MRI shows a prostate volume of 70 mL with a single PI-RADS 3 lesion, giving a PSA density of 0.07 µg/L/mL. Digital rectal examination is unremarkable. He has no family history of prostate cancer.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate interpretation?
options: Biopsy is required for any PI-RADS 3 lesion
Proceed to radical prostatectomy for a likely cancer
A PSMA PET scan is needed to characterise the lesion
Discharge from follow-up because PI-RADS 3 is benign
Biopsy is not routinely needed; continue PSA monitoring
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

E. Biopsy is not routinely needed; continue PSA monitoring

---

The 2026 Australian early detection guideline recommends biopsy for PI-RADS 4–5 lesions, or for PI-RADS 3 lesions when PSA density is 0.15 or more. With PI-RADS 3 and a PSA density of 0.07, the risk of clinically significant cancer is low, so the guideline says biopsy may not be required, subject to clinical assessment. Ongoing monitoring is appropriate. The higher PSA is explained by his large gland.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
PI-RADS 3 lesion: biopsy if PSA density is ≥0.15. Below that, monitor.

---

question_text:
A 45-year-old man sees his GP in Darwin, NT. His father was diagnosed with prostate cancer at 58. He has no urinary symptoms. After discussing the benefits and harms of testing, he decides he wants to be tested.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate testing approach?
options: Wait until he is 50
PSA test now, repeated every 2 years
Annual PSA with digital rectal examination
mpMRI prostate as the first screening test
Germline BRCA testing before any PSA
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

B. PSA test now, repeated every 2 years

---

The 2026 Australian early detection guideline proposes offering PSA testing every 2 years from age 45 to men at higher risk who choose testing after discussing benefits and harms. Higher risk includes a family history of prostate cancer, men of Black sub-Saharan African ancestry, and confirmed BRCA2 carriers. Men aged 50–69 at average risk are offered PSA testing every 2 years.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Men at higher risk (family history, BRCA2, Black African ancestry) can be offered PSA every 2 years from age 45.

A 57-year-old man in Ballarat, Vic, chose PSA testing after discussing it with his GP. His result is 3.6 µg/L. He has no urinary symptoms, no recent urinary infection and no family history of prostate cancer. Urine dipstick is normal.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate next step?
options: Refer now for a systematic transrectal biopsy
Reassure him because the PSA is below 4.0 µg/L
Repeat the PSA in 2 years at his usual interval
Start finasteride and recheck the PSA in 6 months
Repeat the PSA within 1-3 months, then refer if still 3.0 or more
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

E. Repeat the PSA within 1-3 months, then refer if still 3.0 or more

---

The 2026 Australian early detection guideline says that if total PSA is 3.0 µg/L or more, the test should be repeated within 1–3 months. If the result is confirmed, offer referral and further investigation, with mpMRI before biopsy.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
PSA of 3.0 µg/L or more: repeat within 1–3 months and, if confirmed, refer for further investigation.

---

question_text:
A 55-year-old woman is admitted to a hospital in Wagga Wagga, NSW, with gallstone pancreatitis. On admission her lipase was 4,800 U/L (<60). At 48 hours her lipase has fallen to 900 U/L and her CRP is 240 mg/L. A registrar suggests she is improving because her lipase has fallen.

Which one of the following is the most accurate interpretation?
options: CRP above 150 at 48 hours predicts severe disease despite the falling lipase
The falling lipase shows the pancreatitis is resolving
The very high admission lipase predicted severe disease
Daily lipase should be used to guide feeding and discharge
CRP is unhelpful because it rises with any inflammation
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

A. CRP above 150 at 48 hours predicts severe disease despite the falling lipase

---

Australian Prescriber notes that neither amylase nor lipase helps monitor or predict the severity of pancreatitis in adults, and the size of the rise does not predict severity. Daily measurements should not be used to judge disease activity. A CRP above 150 mg/L at 48 hours after symptom onset is the best single laboratory predictor of severity, alongside composite scores.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
In adult pancreatitis, a CRP above 150 mg/L at 48 hours predicts severity. Lipase levels do not.

---

question_text:
A 38-year-old farm worker in Gympie, Qld, has a deep laceration to his right thigh from a chainsaw. Bright red blood is spurting from the wound despite firm direct pressure with a pad from a colleague. He is pale and sweaty, with a pulse of 130/min. An ambulance has been called, and a commercial windlass tourniquet is in the first aid kit. The colleague is trained in its use.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate immediate action?
options: Elevate the leg and continue firm direct pressure
Apply an elastic venous tourniquet above the knee
Position the airway before attempting bleeding control
Apply the arterial tourniquet above the wound and note the time
Remove the pad every few minutes to inspect the wound
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

D. Apply the arterial tourniquet above the wound and note the time

---

ANZCOR Guideline 9.1.1 states that firm direct pressure is the most effective way to stop most bleeding. Where life-threatening limb bleeding is not controlled by direct pressure, an arterial tourniquet is suggested if one is available and the first aider is trained in its use. It is applied above the bleeding point (5 cm above if there are no manufacturer instructions), not over a joint, and tightened until the bleeding stops. The time is recorded and passed on, and the tourniquet is not removed until the person reaches specialist care.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
If life-threatening limb bleeding continues despite pressure, apply an arterial tourniquet above the wound and record the time.

---

question_text:
A 26-year-old chef in Fremantle, WA, spilt boiling water over his left forearm 40 minutes ago. He ran it under the tap for about two minutes and then wrapped it in a towel. He now attends the emergency department with a painful, blistered, red area about the size of his palm.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate immediate first aid?
options: Apply ice packs for 10 minutes
Cool the burn under cool running water for 20 minutes
Apply a burn cream and dressing; it is too late for cooling
Pop the blisters and dress the wound
Cool for 5 minutes only, to avoid hypothermia
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

B. Cool the burn under cool running water for 20 minutes

---

ANZCOR Guideline 9.1.3 recommends cooling burns with cool running water for at least 20 minutes, as soon as possible. Cooling still helps when started up to 3 hours after the burn. Afterwards, cover loosely with a non-stick dressing such as cling film. Ice, creams and breaking blisters should be avoided.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Burn first aid: at least 20 minutes of cool running water, effective up to 3 hours after the burn. No ice.

---

incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Intact blisters protect the wound from infection; ANZCOR advises not to break them.

question_text:
A 61-year-old man in Rockhampton, Qld, has had sudden severe upper abdominal pain for four hours. He takes naproxen for back pain. He has a rigid abdomen with generalised guarding. Pulse 108/min, BP 112/70 mmHg. An erect chest X-ray done in the department shows no free gas under the diaphragm.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate next investigation?
options: Reassure: perforation is excluded by the chest X-ray
CT abdomen and pelvis
Left lateral decubitus X-ray first, then decide
Upper GI endoscopy
Abdominal ultrasound
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

B. CT abdomen and pelvis

---

The WSES perforated peptic ulcer guideline notes that a negative X-ray does not rule out perforation. When there are clear signs of peritonitis, abdominal CT should be the first imaging test. CT shows free extraluminal gas and fluid and can help locate the perforation, so a normal erect X-ray should not delay CT and surgical review.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Suspected perforation with peritonitis: go to CT. A normal erect chest X-ray does not exclude it.

---

question_text:
A 31-year-old woman in her second pregnancy attends her GP in Toowoomba, Qld, at 21 weeks' gestation. She had a dTpa vaccine during her first pregnancy two years ago and asks whether she needs another.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate advice?
options: No vaccine is needed because she had one 2 years ago
Give dTpa at 36 weeks, closer to the birth
Vaccinate the baby at birth instead of the mother
Give dTpa now; it is recommended in every pregnancy
Give dTpa to her after the birth (postpartum)
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

D. Give dTpa now; it is recommended in every pregnancy

---

The Australian Immunisation Handbook recommends a single dose of pertussis-containing vaccine (dTpa) in each pregnancy, ideally between 20 and 32 weeks' gestation, whatever the time since a previous dose. This maximises the transfer of maternal antibodies to protect the newborn.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
dTpa in every pregnancy, ideally at 20–32 weeks.

question_text:
A 22-year-old woman at 14 weeks' gestation in Cairns, Qld, has a positive chlamydia NAAT on her first-pass urine at her antenatal booking visit. She has been given azithromycin 1 g orally as a single dose. Her partner has been contacted for treatment.

Which one of the following follow-up tests is most appropriate?
options: No further testing after single-dose azithromycin
Test of cure NAAT 1 week after treatment
Chlamydia serology at 6 weeks
Test of cure NAAT at 4 weeks, then retest at 3 months
Endocervical culture only at delivery
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

D. Test of cure NAAT at 4 weeks, then retest at 3 months

---

The Australian STI Management Guidelines recommend a test of cure for chlamydia in pregnancy, done at least 4 weeks after treatment so that residual non-viable DNA does not give a false-positive result. All people with chlamydia should also be retested at 3 months to detect reinfection.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Chlamydia in pregnancy: test of cure at 4 weeks or more after treatment, then retest at 3 months.

---

question_text:
A 34-year-old woman in Alice Springs, NT, has had a frothy yellow-green vaginal discharge and vulval itch for one week. Speculum examination shows a punctate erythematous cervix. She has a new partner.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate test to confirm the likely diagnosis?
options: Wet-mount microscopy only
Trichomonas vaginalis NAAT on a vaginal swab
High vaginal swab culture for Candida
Serology for Trichomonas
Gram stain for clue cells
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

B. Trichomonas vaginalis NAAT on a vaginal swab

---

The Australian STI Management Guidelines recommend NAAT (PCR) for Trichomonas vaginalis because it is far more sensitive than wet-mount microscopy. A positive result is treated with metronidazole 400 mg twice daily for 7 days (or 2 g stat as an alternative), along with treatment of her partner and testing for other STIs.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Trichomoniasis is diagnosed by NAAT.

---

question_text:
A 32-year-old woman in Newcastle, NSW, has a pelvic ultrasound for an unrelated reason. It shows a 3.2 cm unilocular, thin-walled, anechoic left ovarian cyst with no solid components, septations or internal blood flow. She has no symptoms, and her periods are regular.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate interpretation?
options: Measure CA-125 and refer to a gynaecological oncologist
Laparoscopic cystectomy
Repeat ultrasound every 3 months for 2 years
Almost certainly a benign functional cyst; no follow-up is needed
MRI pelvis
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

D. Almost certainly a benign functional cyst; no follow-up is needed

---

An Australian Family Physician review of ovarian masses states that a simple anechoic cyst smaller than 5 cm in a premenopausal woman is almost certainly benign (often functional) and needs no follow-up. CA-125 is not needed in premenopausal women unless the ultrasound features are suspicious.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
A simple cyst under 5 cm in a premenopausal woman is benign and needs no follow-up.

A 27-year-old woman in Geelong, Vic, has a thin, grey, malodorous vaginal discharge that is worse after intercourse. She has no itch or dysuria. The vulva and cervix look normal.

Bedside findings:
- Vaginal pH 5.2
- Adding potassium hydroxide gives a fishy odour
- Gram stain: clue cells with loss of lactobacilli

Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Vulvovaginal candidiasis
Trichomoniasis
Bacterial vaginosis
Physiological discharge
Chlamydial cervicitis
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

C. Bacterial vaginosis

---

The Australian STI Management Guidelines describe bacterial vaginosis as a thin grey or white discharge with a fishy odour, a vaginal pH above 4.5 and a positive whiff test. Microscopy or Gram stain shows clue cells and depletion of lactobacilli.

---

BV: pH above 4.5, positive whiff test and clue cells.

question_text:
A 38-year-old woman in Launceston, Tas, has a 6 cm left adnexal mass found on transvaginal ultrasound for pelvic discomfort. The ultrasound describes a multilocular cyst with a solid papillary projection. She has no family history of ovarian cancer.

Which one of the following investigations is most appropriate next?
options: No test; repeat the ultrasound in 6 months
Serum CA-125, because the ultrasound features are suspicious
Serum hCG only
Laparoscopic aspiration of the cyst
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

C. Serum CA-125, because the ultrasound features are suspicious

---

The Australian Family Physician review advises that in premenopausal women, CA-125 should be measured only when ultrasound shows suspicious features, because it is raised by many benign conditions such as endometriosis and menstruation. Solid papillary projections in a multilocular cyst are suspicious. The result guides referral, including possible gynaecological oncology review.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
In premenopausal women, measure CA-125 only if the ultrasound is suspicious.

---

question_text:
A 2-year-old boy is brought to an emergency department in Bendigo, Vic, with 24 hours of diarrhoea and vomiting. He has moderate dehydration: dry mucous membranes, reduced urine output and slightly sunken eyes. He has refused or vomited small, frequent amounts of oral rehydration solution given over the last hour despite ondansetron. He is alert, with normal perfusion.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate next step?
options: Nasogastric rehydration with oral rehydration solution
IV fluid bolus
Loperamide
Switch to diluted apple juice and keep trying orally
Admit and keep nil by mouth
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

A. Nasogastric rehydration with oral rehydration solution

---

The RCH Gastroenteritis guideline recommends oral rehydration solution first. If oral rehydration fails and there is an ongoing risk of dehydration, rapid or slow NG rehydration may be appropriate. If NG is not tolerated, the child should have IV rehydration if clinically dehydrated. Breastfeeding should continue.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
In paediatric gastroenteritis, if ORS fails, use NG rehydration before IV fluids (and IV if NG is not tolerated).

---

question_text:
A 4-year-old girl weighing 17 kg is seen in an emergency department in Albury, NSW, with gastroenteritis. She has mild dehydration and keeps vomiting with every attempt to drink oral rehydration solution.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate antiemetic plan?
options: Oral ondansetron 8 mg once, then retry ORS
IV metoclopramide 0.15 mg/kg once
Oral ondansetron 4 mg once, then retry ORS
Rectal prochlorperazine suppository
No antiemetic; antiemetics are contraindicated in children
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

C. Oral ondansetron 4 mg once, then retry ORS

---

The RCH Gastroenteritis guideline says a single dose of ondansetron can be given to support hydration in children over 6 months with persistent nausea or vomiting. The weight-based doses are 8–15 kg: 2 mg; 15–30 kg: 4 mg; over 30 kg: 8 mg. A 17 kg child gets 4 mg.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Ondansetron in children over 6 months: 2 mg (8–15 kg), 4 mg (15–30 kg), 8 mg (over 30 kg).

question_text:
A 3-year-old girl in Mackay, Qld, has had right ear pain and a fever of 38.4 °C since yesterday. Otoscopy shows a red, bulging right tympanic membrane with no discharge. She is well, eating and drinking, and has no other medical problems. She is not an Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander child.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate management?
options: Oral amoxicillin for 10 days
Regular paracetamol or ibuprofen; no antibiotics
Ear wick with topical antibiotic drops
Urgent ENT referral for myringotomy
Oral prednisolone with a decongestant
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

B. Regular paracetamol or ibuprofen; no antibiotics

---

The RCH Acute otitis media guideline states that most cases of AOM in children resolve without treatment and antibiotics are not recommended. Uncomplicated AOM in a well child: regular simple analgesia, no antibiotics.

question_text:
A 6-year-old boy in Ipswich, Qld, has had infrequent hard stools for 8 months and recent soiling of his underwear. Abdominal examination shows a palpable faecal mass. He has no red flags: normal growth, normal neurological examination of the lower limbs, and meconium passed in the first day of life.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate initial management?
options: Oral high-dose macrogol disimpaction at home, then maintenance
Phosphate enema in the clinic today
Glycerol suppositories daily for a week
Increase dietary fibre and fluids alone
Abdominal X-ray to confirm faecal loading first
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

A. Oral high-dose macrogol disimpaction at home, then maintenance

---

Rectal treatment with suppositories or enemas should be avoided (at most a one-off dose may be considered). Once disimpaction is achieved, maintenance treatment should start immediately and continue, along with behavioural measures such as toilet routines.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Paediatric faecal impaction: oral macrogol disimpaction, then maintenance immediately. Avoid enemas.

---

question_text:
An 18-month-old girl is brought to a GP clinic in Broome, WA, with two days of diarrhoea. Her mother is worried about dehydration. The child's health record shows she was weighed at a clinic visit 5 days ago, before she became unwell.

Which one of the following is the most accurate way to assess her degree of dehydration?
options: Compare her weight now with her recent pre-illness weight
Capillary refill time measured centrally on the sternum
Serum urea, creatinine and bicarbonate
Urine specific gravity on a bag specimen
Presence or absence of tears when she cries
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

A. Compare her weight now with her recent pre-illness weight

---

The RCH Dehydration guideline states that the difference between pre-morbid weight and current weight is the most accurate assessment of dehydration. If a recent weight (within 2 weeks) is not available, history and examination are used to estimate dehydration.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
The change from pre-illness weight is the most accurate measure of dehydration.

---

question_text:
A 5-year-old boy falls from a 1-metre playground platform in Wollongong, NSW, and bumps his forehead. His father saw a brief loss of consciousness lasting a few seconds before he cried. He has not vomited and has no headache. He now has a GCS of 15 and is playing, with a small frontal haematoma. He has no bleeding disorder, takes no anticoagulants, has no VP shunt and has no neurodevelopmental disorder.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate approach?
options: Immediate CT brain because he lost consciousness
Discharge home now with a head injury advice sheet
Observe with regular neuro obs; CT if he deteriorates
Skull X-ray to look for a fracture
MRI brain under general anaesthetic today
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

C. Observe with regular neuro obs; CT if he deteriorates

---

The RCH Head injury guideline lists a history of loss of consciousness as a relative indication for imaging. If more than one relative indication is present, the child is observed and neuroimaging is considered. For a mild head injury with a risk factor, the child is observed for up to 4 hours after the injury, with 30-minutely neurological observations for the first 2 hours and then hourly. A persistent headache, ongoing vomiting, a GCS of 14 or persistent altered mental status means further observation and likely investigation. He can go home once he has been back to a normal conscious state for at least an hour, is acting normally and is tolerating fluids.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Mild head injury with a single risk factor: observe for up to 4 hours with neurological observations, and image if he deteriorates.

---

question_text:
A 3-year-old boy with atopic dermatitis is brought to a clinic in Toowoomba, Qld. For two days he has had rapidly spreading, painful clusters of monomorphic punched-out erosions on his face and neck, with some small vesicles. He has a fever of 38.6 °C and is irritable. His eczema had been flaring.

Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Impetiginised eczema
Eczema herpeticum
Eczema flare only
Varicella
Contact dermatitis
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

B. Eczema herpeticum

---

Monomorphic punched-out erosions and vesicles appearing in an area of active eczema, with fever and systemic upset, are typical of eczema herpeticum (disseminated HSV). The RCH Eczema guideline lists this as a complication needing prompt antiviral treatment (IV in severe cases), with consultation with the paediatric team. Periorbital involvement needs urgent ophthalmology review.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Punched-out erosions in eczematous skin with fever suggest eczema herpeticum, which needs prompt antiviral treatment.

---

question_text:
A 39-year-old man with treatment-resistant schizophrenia has been stable on clozapine 400 mg daily for two years under shared care. He sees his GP in Logan, Qld, for a routine review. His blood monitoring is up to date and normal. He says he feels 'fine' and has no complaints.

Which one of the following is the most important additional history to take at this visit?
options: Bowel habit, including frequency and straining
Family history of schizophrenia or psychosis
Childhood developmental and school history
Daily caffeine intake
Night sweats and weight loss
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

A. Bowel habit, including frequency and straining

---

Australian Prescriber notes that constipation affects 15–60% of people on clozapine at any time, is potentially life-threatening and should be treated and prevented aggressively. Clozapine-induced gastrointestinal hypomotility can progress to obstruction or ileus. Patients often do not volunteer symptoms, so bowel habit should be asked about at every review, and preventive aperients started at the first sign of constipation.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Ask every patient on clozapine about bowel habit. Constipation is common and can be fatal.

question_text:
A 45-year-old woman in Bunbury, WA, stopped venlafaxine 225 mg daily abruptly four days ago after 3 years of treatment because she felt well. She now has dizziness, 'electric shock' sensations in her head when she moves her eyes, vivid dreams, irritability and tearfulness. She has no suicidal thoughts. Her symptoms began within 48 hours of stopping.

Which one of the following is the most likely explanation?
options: Relapse of major depression
Serotonin syndrome
Vestibular neuritis
Hypomania
Antidepressant withdrawal symptoms
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

E. Antidepressant withdrawal symptoms

---

The Australian Prescriber article on stopping antidepressants (2026) describes withdrawal symptoms that include physical symptoms (dizziness, sensitivity to light and sound, 'brain zaps' or electric shock sensations, vivid dreams, akathisia) and emotional symptoms (anxiety, irritability, low mood, tearfulness). Abrupt cessation, longer duration of therapy and certain drugs (venlafaxine, duloxetine, paroxetine) raise the risk. Her rapid onset after stopping, with brain zaps, points to withdrawal rather than relapse.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Brain zaps, dizziness and mood symptoms soon after abruptly stopping venlafaxine suggest withdrawal.

---

question_text:
A 30-year-old man in Canberra, ACT, has taken sertraline 100 mg daily for 9 months for a first episode of depression, which is now in full remission. After discussing it with his GP, he wants to stop. He has never had difficulty stopping a medication before.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate plan?
options: Stop sertraline today
Taper over 12 months in 1 mg steps using liquid
Switch to fluoxetine 20 mg for 2 days, then stop
Halve the dose every day over 4 days, then stop
Reduce by 25-50% steps every 2 weeks, then stop
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

E. Reduce by 25-50% steps every 2 weeks, then stop

---

Australian Prescriber (2026) states that in patients at low risk of withdrawal symptoms, guidelines recommend 25 to 50% dose reductions over 2 to 6 weeks, for example sertraline tapered at 2-weekly intervals from 100 mg to 50 mg, then 25 mg, then stopped. Patients at higher risk may need smaller reductions over months.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Low-risk antidepressant cessation: reduce by 25–50% over 2–6 weeks.

---

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Stopping abruptly can cause withdrawal symptoms.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: This is for higher-risk patients or those who have had difficulty stopping before.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: This is not the recommended approach for a low-risk patient.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Daily halving stops the drug within days, which is too fast to prevent withdrawal symptoms; reductions are usually spaced about 2 weeks apart.

question_text:
A 26-year-old woman in Darwin, NT, has a new diagnosis of bipolar I disorder after a manic episode, which has been treated as an inpatient. She is not pregnant, is sexually active and may want children in future. The psychiatry registrar is choosing a long-term mood stabiliser and suggests sodium valproate because it worked quickly for her uncle.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate response regarding valproate?
options: Valproate is the preferred first-line option for women of reproductive age
Valproate is acceptable as long as she also takes folic acid 5 mg
Valproate is safe provided it is stopped once pregnancy is confirmed
Valproate restrictions apply to epilepsy, not to bipolar disorder
Avoid valproate unless other treatments fail or are not tolerated
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

E. Avoid valproate unless other treatments fail or are not tolerated

---

The Australian Epilim (sodium valproate) Product Information states that valproate should not be used in female children and women of childbearing potential unless other treatments are ineffective or not tolerated. This is because valproate has a high teratogenic potential, and children exposed in utero have a high risk of congenital malformations and neurodevelopmental disorders. Treatment must be started and supervised by a specialist. Other options should be used first.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Avoid valproate in women of childbearing potential unless other treatments are ineffective or not tolerated.

---

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: The Australian PI states the opposite: valproate should not be used in women of childbearing potential unless other treatments are ineffective or not tolerated.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: High-dose folic acid does not prevent valproate-related neurodevelopmental harm and only partly reduces neural tube risk.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Exposure in early pregnancy carries the risk.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: The teratogenic risk and PI restriction apply to every indication, including bipolar disorder.

question_text:
A 48-year-old woman on clozapine 500 mg daily is brought to an emergency department in Shepparton, Vic. She has had three days of abdominal distension, colicky pain and vomiting, and today passed watery stools. Temperature 38.0 °C, pulse 118/min. Her abdomen is distended and tender, with absent bowel sounds. She also takes oxybutynin. Her neutrophil count is 6.4 × 10^9/L.

Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Viral gastroenteritis
Clozapine-induced agranulocytosis with neutropenic enterocolitis
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome
Irritable bowel syndrome
Clozapine-induced gastrointestinal hypomotility with ileus
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

E. Clozapine-induced gastrointestinal hypomotility with ileus

---

Australian Prescriber lists red flags of serious clozapine-induced constipation: abdominal pain, distension, vomiting, overflow diarrhoea, absent bowel sounds, and signs or symptoms of sepsis. Anticholinergic drugs such as oxybutynin add to the risk and should be avoided when possible. This needs urgent hospital assessment.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Clozapine plus pain, distension, vomiting, overflow diarrhoea and absent bowel sounds suggests hypomotility or ileus, which is an emergency.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "Australian Prescriber. Clozapine in primary care", "url": "https://australianprescriber.tg.org.au/articles/clozapine-in-primary-care.html"}
subtopic: Red flags of clozapine-induced gastrointestinal hypomotility

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Absent bowel sounds and distension in a patient on clozapine point to hypomotility. The 'diarrhoea' is likely overflow.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Neutropenic enterocolitis needs neutropenia; her neutrophil count is normal.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: There is no rigidity or altered mental state.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: IBS is a chronic functional disorder; it never causes fever, tachycardia, distension with absent bowel sounds or vomiting.

key_takeaways: Clozapine plus pain, distension, vomiting, overflow diarrhoea and absent bowel sounds suggests hypomotility or ileus, which is an emergency.

question_text:
A 22-year-old man with first-episode schizophrenia in Wollongong, NSW, is to start olanzapine after a shared decision with his psychiatrist. His BMI is 24 kg/m², and his fasting glucose and lipids are normal. He is worried about weight gain.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate additional measure at the time of starting olanzapine?
options: Wait until he has gained 7% of body weight before acting
Start orlistat
Add topiramate routinely
Start metformin at the same time, alongside lifestyle advice
No measures because his BMI is normal
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

D. Start metformin at the same time, alongside lifestyle advice

---

The RANZCP-endorsed INTEGRATE guidelines recommend lifestyle interventions for everyone and co-initiating metformin when starting antipsychotics with high metabolic risk, such as olanzapine or clozapine, to limit weight gain.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
INTEGRATE: co-initiate metformin with olanzapine or clozapine.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "RANZCP. INTEGRATE: international guidelines for the algorithmic treatment of schizophrenia", "url": "https://www.ranzcp.org/clinical-guidelines-publications/clinical-guidelines-publications-library/integrate-international-guidelines-for-the-algorithmic-treatment-of-schizophrenia"}
subtopic: Starting olanzapine: co-initiate metformin to limit weight gain

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: INTEGRATE recommends preventive co-initiation of metformin.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Orlistat is a weight-loss drug for obesity; it is not recommended to prevent antipsychotic-induced weight gain.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Topiramate has some evidence for weight reduction but is not the recommended preventive agent and has cognitive side effects.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: Olanzapine causes predictable weight gain, especially in first-episode patients, so prevention starts at initiation regardless of baseline BMI.

key_takeaways: INTEGRATE: co-initiate metformin with olanzapine or clozapine.

INTEGRATE: international guidelines for the algorithmic treatment of schizophrenia", "url": "https://www.ranzcp.org/clinical-guidelines-publications/clinical-guidelines-publications-library/integrate-international-guidelines-for-the-algorithmic-treatment-of-schizophrenia"}

question_text:
In a stable population in regional Victoria, the incidence of a chronic skin condition is 4 new cases per 1,000 person-years. The average duration of the condition is 5 years. Assume steady state and low prevalence.

Which one of the following is the best estimate of the prevalence?
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

B. 20 per 1,000

---

At steady state with low prevalence, prevalence ≈ incidence × average duration = 4/1,000 per year × 5 years = 20 per 1,000 (2%).

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Prevalence ≈ incidence × duration (steady state, rare disease).

---

REFERENCES

incorrect_answer_explanations.C: This is the incidence rate, which ignores how long people remain cases.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: This adds incidence and duration (4 + 5), which has no epidemiological meaning.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: This is a tenfold slip (40 cases x 5 years per 1,000); 4/1,000 x 5 = 20/1,000.

question_text:
A cohort study in Adelaide follows 200 disease-free workers. 100 workers are followed for 4 years each and 100 for 2 years each (losses to follow-up). Over the study, 12 develop occupational asthma.

Which one of the following is the incidence rate?
options: 60 per 1,000 people
15 per 1,000 person-years
20 per 1,000 person-years
30 per 1,000 person-years
12 per 1,000 person-years
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

C. 20 per 1,000 person-years

---

Person-time = 100 × 4 + 100 × 2 = 600 person-years. Incidence rate = 12/600 = 0.02 per person-year = 20 per 1,000 person-years.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Incidence rate = new cases ÷ total person-time at risk.

---

REFERENCES

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: This is the cumulative proportion (12/200) and ignores person-time.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: This uses 800 person-years, as if all 200 workers were followed for 4 years; losses to follow-up contribute only the time actually observed.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: This uses only the 400 person-years from the workers followed for 4 years and ignores the 200 from those lost.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: This divides 12 cases by 1,000 rather than by the 600 person-years observed.

question_text:
A public health unit in Queensland is modelling an outbreak of a vaccine-preventable infection with a basic reproduction number (R0) of 5. Assume homogeneous mixing and a vaccine that gives complete, lasting protection.

Which one of the following is the minimum proportion of the population that must be immune to prevent sustained transmission?
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

A. 80%

---

Herd immunity threshold = 1 − 1/R0 = 1 − 1/5 = 0.8, or 80%. If vaccine effectiveness is below 100%, the coverage needed is higher (threshold ÷ effectiveness).

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Herd immunity threshold = 1 − 1/R0.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "Herd immunity. Current Biology 2021 (primer)", "url": "https://www.cell.com/current-biology/fulltext/S0960-9822(21)00039-7"}
subtopic: Herd immunity threshold from R0

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: This is 1/R0, the proportion that may remain susceptible, not the proportion that must be immune.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: 50% would only be the threshold if R0 were 2.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: This is the threshold for a much higher R0, as with measles.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: Herd immunity does not require full immunity.

key_takeaways: Herd immunity threshold = 1 − 1/R0.

question_text:
An analysis of Australian local government areas shows that areas with higher average household fluoride filter sales have higher rates of dental caries in children. A councillor concludes that children in households that buy fluoride filters are more likely to develop caries.

Which one of the following best describes the main problem with this conclusion?
options: Recall bias
Lead-time bias
Ecological fallacy
Berkson bias
Healthy worker effect
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

C. Ecological fallacy

---

The data are aggregated at area level. Applying an association seen between groups to individuals is the ecological fallacy, because the children with caries may not be in the households that bought filters. Individual-level data are needed to support this inference.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Group-level associations cannot be assumed to hold for individuals (ecological fallacy).

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "Understanding the ecological fallacy. BMJ 2015;351:h4773", "url": "https://www.bmj.com/content/351/bmj.h4773"}
subtopic: Ecological fallacy

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Recall bias arises when cases and controls remember exposures differently; these are routine area-level sales data, not recall.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Lead-time bias is an apparent survival benefit from earlier diagnosis by screening; no screening or survival is involved.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Berkson bias is selection bias from studying hospitalised patients; the analysis uses whole local government areas.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: The healthy worker effect applies to occupational cohorts compared with the general population.

key_takeaways: Group-level associations cannot be assumed to hold for individuals (ecological fallacy).
guideline_reference: {"name": "Understanding the ecological fallacy. BMJ 2015;351:h4773", "url": "https://www.bmj.com/content/351/bmj.h4773"}

question_text:
A 40-year-old man in Lismore, NSW, was scratched on the forearm this morning while removing a live microbat from his shed. He has never had rabies vaccine. He has captured the bat in a box, and the local public health unit says a lyssavirus result can be available within 24 hours. He has washed the wound well with soap and water.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate next step?
options: Release the bat outdoors and start full PEP today
Test the bat for ABLV and withhold PEP until the result
Start HRIG and rabies vaccine now regardless of testing
No action because it was only a scratch, not a bite
Check his rabies antibody titre to decide on PEP
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

B. Test the bat for ABLV and withhold PEP until the result

---

The Australian Immunisation Handbook advises that, if possible, the bat should be kept and tested for Australian bat lyssavirus. After wound management, HRIG and rabies vaccine are withheld if the bat's ABLV status will be available within 48 hours of the exposure. If not, PEP starts as soon as possible. Bites to the head and neck are an exception: PEP is given promptly, preferably within 48 hours, even if the animal is being tested. If the bat tests negative, no PEP is needed.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
After a bat exposure, test the bat. If the result will be available within 48 hours (and there is no head or neck bite), PEP can wait.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "Australian Immunisation Handbook. Rabies and other lyssaviruses", "url": "https://immunisationhandbook.health.gov.au/contents/vaccine-preventable-diseases/rabies-and-other-lyssaviruses"}

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Releasing a captured bat removes the chance to test it; a negative result avoids unnecessary HRIG and vaccine.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: With a result due within 48 hours and a limb wound, PEP can be withheld.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Bat scratches are category II or III exposures.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: Serology is not used to decide on PEP for an unvaccinated person.

key_takeaways: After a bat exposure, test the bat. If the result will be available within 48 hours (and there is no head or neck bite), PEP can wait.

question_text:
A 52-year-old wildlife carer in Townsville, Qld, was bitten through the skin on the hand by a flying fox two days ago. The bat escaped and cannot be tested. She has never had rabies vaccine and is immunocompetent. The wound has been washed.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate post-exposure prophylaxis?
options: Rabies vaccine on days 0 and 3 only
No PEP, because Australia is free of rabies
HRIG into the wound alone, without vaccine
Five vaccine doses with serology afterwards
HRIG into the wound plus vaccine on days 0, 3, 7, 14
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

E. HRIG into the wound plus vaccine on days 0, 3, 7, 14

---

The Australian Immunisation Handbook bat-exposure algorithm states that a non-immune, immunocompetent person with a category II or III bat exposure should receive HRIG (if 7 days or less since the first vaccine dose) and 4 vaccine doses intramuscularly on days 0, 3, 7 and 14. HRIG is infiltrated in and around the wound as much as possible, with any remainder given intramuscularly away from the vaccine site.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Non-immune, immunocompetent person with a bat bite: HRIG plus 4 vaccine doses (days 0, 3, 7, 14).

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "Australian Immunisation Handbook. Rabies and other lyssaviruses", "url": "https://immunisationhandbook.health.gov.au/contents/vaccine-preventable-diseases/rabies-and-other-lyssaviruses"}

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Australia is free of classical rabies, but Australian bats carry Australian bat lyssavirus, which causes fatal rabies-like disease; PEP is the same.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: HRIG gives short-term passive protection only; vaccine is always needed to produce active immunity.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: This is the regimen for immunocompromised people.
